Applied to the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we evaluate our learned brain embeddings on the downstream tasks of brain captioning and image reconstruction, as well as cross-participant generalization. Our self-supervised approach achieves competitive performance with parameter-rich supervised pipelines that are trained end-to-end with access to image and language data. We further find that encoders trained independently for different participants can be aligned fully unsupervised, using neither images nor stimuli shared between them. After alignment, a neural decoding head trained on one participant can be applied to another without fine-tuning and retains most of its within-subject performance on image reconstruction and brain captioning. By removing the need for images and shared stimuli, our approach is a step towards pooling fMRI data across participants and, eventually, across datasets.
items.title_ko: 잠재 예측을 통한 감각 유발 fMRI 데이터의 교차 피험자 정렬 가능 표현 학습
items.summary_ko: 이 연구는 자기 지도 학습(SSL)이 감각 유발 기능성 자기공명영상(fMRI) 데이터에서 강력한 다운스트림 성능을 지원하는 표현을 생성할 수 있는지 탐구합니다. Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA)를 변형하여 뇌 데이터만을 사용하여 참가자별 인코더를 훈련합니다. 이 인코더들은 자극 이미지나 이미지에서 파생된 어떠한 표현도 보지 않고 훈련됩니다.
items.why_ko: 뇌 영상 데이터 분석에서 자기 지도 학습의 가능성을 탐구하여, 복잡한 뇌 데이터에서 유의미한 패턴을 추출하는 새로운 방법을 제시합니다.

items.title: Neighborhood Elites: Quality-Diversity Search for Uncertainty Quantification in Question Answering
items.body: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, yet they produce wrong answers indistinguishable from correct ones. In question answering (QA), such an error propagates unnoticed into downstream tasks. Perturbation-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) addresses this by probing a model over a set of input rewrites and reading uncertainty from how much its predictions vary. Yet this set is usually built generically, by free paraphrasing, token-level perturbation, or adversarial search. Such rewrites leave two things uncontrolled that matter in QA: what kind of change is made to the context, and how explicitly the context supports the answer. When neither is controlled, the composition of the set is determined by the generator rather than by design, and the estimate inherits whatever that generator happens to produce. Quality-diversity (QD) search is built to cover a predefined exploration space, so we recast input perturbation as a QD problem and propose \emph{neighborhood elites (NE)}, a neighborhood constructor that spreads answer-preserving rewrites across two axes, the kind of edit and the explicitness of support. We compare NE against three other neighborhood constructors, holding the editor, QA model, uncertainty measure and search objective fixed, and against three scores read from the original context. Across five extractive-QA datasets and five instruction-tuned LLMs, NE improves failure detection against every other constructor in at least 24 of the 25 dataset-model pairs, reaching 0.726 AUROC and 0.211 AUPRC lift over the base rate. Additionally, NE detects failure better than semantic entropy computed over decoder samples, by 0.074 AUROC and 0.062 AUPRC lift, and this advantage widens as the neighborhood grows.
items.title_ko: 질의응답 모델의 불확실성 정량화를 위한 이웃 엘리트(Neighborhood Elites) 기반 Quality-Diversity 탐색
items.summary_ko: 대규모 언어 모델(LLM)은 오답을 정답처럼 제시할 수 있어 불확실성 정량화(UQ)가 중요합니다. 이 연구는 입력 재작성을 통해 모델을 탐색하는 섭동 기반 UQ 방식의 한계를 지적하고, 이웃 엘리트(Neighborhood Elites)라는 Quality-Diversity 탐색을 도입합니다. 이 방법은 질문 응답에서 오류의 불확실성을 측정하는 탐색 공간을 보다 효율적으로 구축하여, 모델의 답변 변화를 통해 불확실성을 더 정확하게 파악합니다.
items.why_ko: LLM의 신뢰성을 높이는 데 필수적인 불확실성 정량화 기법을 개선하여, 오답으로 인한 문제 확산을 방지하고 실용적인 LLM 애플리케이션 개발에 기여합니다.

items.title: TaskFrame: Connecting Task-Level Planning with Frame-Level Control for Game Agents
items.body: Building general game agents requires both high-level task reasoning and low-latency action control in rapidly changing visual environments. These capabilities favor models with substantially different computational profiles, making them difficult to realize within a single model. In this work, we present TaskFrame, a hierarchical planner-controller framework that connects task-level planning with frame-level keyboard-and-mouse control. A vision-language task planner decomposes a high-level goal into an ordered sequence of atomic instructions and is optimized through supervised learning and dependency-aware GRPO. The hidden states of special goal tokens that terminate each atomic instruction provide continuous goal embeddings that are cached and reused across control steps. A causal Transformer controller combines the embedding of the active goal with recent observations to predict discrete keyboard and mouse-button actions and continuous camera motion at every game step. We train the system in three stages: planner training, controller pretraining, and joint alignment. Experiments in Minecraft show that TaskFrame is competitive with general-purpose vision-language models on instruction decomposition, and that in closed-loop evaluation the agent achieves a higher combat success rate than the evaluated baselines.
items.title_ko: 게임 에이전트를 위한 TaskFrame: 태스크 수준 계획과 프레임 수준 제어 연결
items.summary_ko: TaskFrame은 일반 게임 에이전트를 위한 계층적 플래너-컨트롤러 프레임워크로, 고수준 태스크 계획과 저지연 키보드-마우스 프레임 수준 제어를 연결합니다. 이 비전-언어 태스크 플래너는 고수준 목표를 서브골로 분해하고, 컨트롤러는 현재 시각 정보를 기반으로 빠른 결정을 내립니다. 이를 통해 복잡하고 빠르게 변화하는 시각 환경에서 효과적인 게임 에이전트 구축이 가능합니다.
items.why_ko: 복잡한 환경에서 AI 에이전트의 일반성을 높이는 중요한 단계로, 고수준 추론과 저수준 제어를 통합하는 실용적인 방법을 제시합니다.

items.title: From MS/MS evidence to adaptive spectroscopic characterization: Reinforcement learning guided by candidate molecular structures
items.body: Small-molecule identification from tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) may require complementary measurements. Herein, we propose a structure-informed deep Q-network (SI-DQN) that uses existing MS/MS evidence to decide whether further characterization is needed, which measurement to request, and when to stop. The policy combines spectral representations and candidate rankings with score-weighted descriptors of the candidates' chemical features and structural differences. The policy was evaluated on 79,462 held-out samples with simulated MS/MS, infrared (IR), and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra from the Multimodal Spectroscopic Dataset. Evaluation used fixed hard candidate sets containing the correct structure and equal normalized acquisition costs. Averaged across three training runs, SI-DQN increased Top-1 accuracy from 80.10% to 93.78% for positive-ion MS/MS starts and from 70.44% to 93.31% for negative-ion starts. The corresponding mean additional measurement counts were only 0.227 and 0.340 per sample, respectively. Complete acquisition achieved 97.72% accuracy with four additions, whereas SI-DQN reduced the additional measurement count by 94.3% and 91.5%. Relative to a rule-based policy, SI-DQN reduced the composite loss combining terminal ranking error and acquisition cost by 19.3% and 25.5%. Adding structural information to DQN further improved accuracy while reducing requests across all three training runs. At comparable ranking uncertainty, SI-DQN increased request rates relative to DQN more strongly in groups with high structural disagreement, where larger reductions in composite loss were also observed. Together, these results support using the ambiguity among candidate structures after MS/MS analysis to guide further characterization, providing a quantitative basis for balancing identification performance against subsequent measurement effort.
items.title_ko: 후보 분자 구조에 의해 유도되는 강화 학습 기반 적응형 분광학적 특성 분석
items.summary_ko: 이 연구는 탠덤 질량 분광법(MS/MS)을 통한 소분자 식별에 필요한 보완 측정 여부, 요청할 측정, 중단 시점을 결정하는 구조 정보 기반 딥 Q-네트워크(SI-DQN)를 제안합니다. 이 정책은 스펙트럼 표현과 후보 순위를 후보의 화학적 특징 및 구조적 차이에 대한 점수 가중치 설명자와 결합합니다. 이를 통해 필요한 추가 측정을 결정하여 분석 효율성을 높입니다.
items.why_ko: 강화 학습을 활용하여 복잡한 과학적 분석 프로세스를 자동화하고 최적화하는 방법을 제시하며, 화학 및 생물학 연구에 기여할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Learned Terminal Costs for Short-Horizon Model Predictive Control of Autonomous Trucks in Interactive Highway Traffic
items.body: Autonomous highway driving for heavy-duty trucks is a challenging control problem. The greater mass, dimensions and intricate dynamics increase the requirements for cooperation from surrounding traffic in critical maneuvers, requiring a careful balance between safety constraints and efficient long-horizon decision making. Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides rigorous constraint satisfaction but relies on terminal cost which can limit its effectiveness at short, computationally affordable horizons. Reinforcement Learning (RL) captures long-term driving behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and tends toward overly conservative policies when trained under sparse collision penalties. In this paper, we propose a hybrid MPC and RL framework for highway driving in autonomous trucks, where a finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, uses a pre-trained RL model for terminal cost estimation. We evaluate the framework in a simulation environment with reactive surrounding traffic and compare it against pure MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with terminal cost estimation using a base policy, and pure RL. Results show that the hybrid approach achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration.
items.title_ko: 대화형 고속도로 교통 환경에서 자율 트럭의 단기 모델 예측 제어 학습 단말 비용
items.summary_ko: 이 연구는 자율 트럭의 고속도로 주행에서 단기 모델 예측 제어(MPC)의 효과를 높이기 위해 학습된 단말 비용을 제안합니다. MPC는 엄격한 제약 만족을 제공하지만, 계산 비용 때문에 단기 예측에 의존해야 합니다. 제안된 접근 방식은 주변 교통과의 상호작용에서 안전 제약과 효율적인 장기 의사 결정 간의 균형을 맞추어 MPC의 성능을 개선합니다.
items.why_ko: 자율주행 시스템의 핵심인 MPC의 성능을 향상시켜, 특히 복잡한 교통 환경에서 자율 트럭의 안전성과 효율성을 높이는 데 기여합니다.

items.title: When Requirements Interact: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding via Interdependent Specifications
items.body: To succeed in real-world long-horizon software development, coding agents must satisfy multi-dimensional task specifications, such as interface compatibility and error handling, and do so without breaking existing dependencies. However, current works lack specification in both quantity and diversity, often emphasizing primary goals while ignoring complex constraints. Synthesizing tasks to bridge this gap presents two challenges: naively adding specifications risks reducing tasks to trivial checklists rather than compelling joint reasoning, and verifying these subtle interactions risks overlooking hidden flaws or rejecting valid alternatives. To address these challenges, we introduce CodeSpecWeave, a framework for synthesizing tasks with rich, interdependent specifications. Grounded in real developer seeds, a synthesis agent iteratively develops both coupled task requirements and executable tests, while a review agent audits solution trajectories from multiple models to guarantee test reliability. Using this pipeline, we construct 4,670 training tasks across 2,865 repositories. Applying Reinforcement learning on these tasks significantly improves performance over the base model on DeepSWE-v1.1, largely outperforming existing baselines. Furthermore, we curate CodeSpecWeave-Bench, a rigorous benchmark comprising 100 tasks and 1,044 specifications, which clearly separates frontier models and reveals significant headroom in handling interdependent engineering constraints.
items.title_ko: 요구사항 상호작용 시 장기 코딩 스케일링: 상호 의존적 사양을 통해
items.summary_ko: 실제 장기 소프트웨어 개발에서 코딩 에이전트는 인터페이스 호환성, 오류 처리 등 다차원적인 태스크 사양을 만족해야 하며, 기존 의존성을 깨뜨리지 않아야 합니다. 이 연구는 상호 의존적 사양(Interdependent Specifications)을 통해 이러한 복잡한 요구사항들을 통합하고, LLM 기반 에이전트가 복잡한 코딩 태스크를 성공적으로 수행하도록 지원하는 새로운 접근 방식을 제시합니다.
items.why_ko: AI 코딩 에이전트의 현실적인 소프트웨어 개발 능력 향상에 기여하며, 복잡한 요구사항을 처리하는 AI 개발의 핵심 과제를 해결하는 데 중요한 연구입니다.

items.title: Statistical Analysis of Synthetic Data with Verification: A Linear Regression Framework
items.body: Synthetic data are widely used for training modern AI systems. However, their statistical understanding remains limited. It is well recognized in statistics that repeated self-training on synthetic data can amplify errors inherited from pre-trained models, leading to model collapse. Verification plays a crucial role in selecting high-quality synthetic data to help prevent model collapse and improve model performance. We study verified self-training in a linear regression framework, where a pre-trained estimator generates synthetic data with injected generation noise and a verifier selects samples according to a verification threshold. Post-training on the accepted samples updates either all coordinates (full fine-tuning) or only an active subset (partial fine-tuning). Our analysis reveals three potentially counterintuitive effects. We establish that tighter verification does not always lead to lower prediction risk. We also find that a suitable level of injected generation noise can reduce prediction risk, while excessive noise can increase it. Moreover, full and partial fine-tuning can respond differently to the same verification rule, since pre-training error in the frozen coordinates affects both sample selection and post-training risk. We analyze these effects by deriving finite sample risk bounds for four separate regimes determined by the relative scales of the verification threshold, generation noise, and pre-training error. The bounds precisely characterize how verification affects prediction risk across these regimes. In particular, we quantify how the generation noise, the effective accepted sample size, and the covariance of the accepted covariates affect prediction risk. The analysis extends to iterative verified full fine-tuning, where sufficiently tight verification reduces the initial error contribution at a geometric rate.
items.title_ko: 검증을 통한 합성 데이터의 통계적 분석: 선형 회귀 프레임워크
items.summary_ko: 합성 데이터는 최신 AI 시스템 훈련에 널리 사용되지만, 통계적 이해는 제한적입니다. 반복적인 합성 데이터 자가 훈련은 사전 훈련된 모델에서 상속된 오류를 증폭시켜 모델 붕괴로 이어질 수 있습니다. 본 연구는 선형 회귀 프레임워크에서 검증된 자가 훈련(verified self-training)을 연구하며, 고품질 합성 데이터 선택이 모델 붕괴를 방지하고 성능을 개선하는 데 중요한 역할을 함을 보여줍니다.
items.why_ko: 모델 붕괴와 같은 합성 데이터 사용의 위험을 줄이고, AI 모델의 신뢰성과 성능을 높이는 데 기여하는 중요한 통계적 기반을 제공합니다.

items.title: Confidence-Aware Speed-over-Ground Estimation from Doppler Spectra via Reconstruction-Based Representation Learning
items.body: Reliable speed-over-ground estimation from ground-facing Doppler spectra is essential for mobile platforms such as railway systems. Classical signal-processing approaches can provide accurate estimates under favorable conditions, but often degrade in challenging conditions. We propose confidence-aware speed-over-ground estimation trained on rail-domain data that estimates speed over ground and frame-level confidence from Doppler spectra with several novel contributions: First, we transfer the idea of exploiting a reconstruction task by an autoencoder for performance estimation from previous work to Doppler RaDAR. Second, we append a speed-over-ground estimation head operating on the autoencoder's latent space features. Third, we omit the reconstruction decoder during inference but add a low-cost dedicated confidence head for frame-wise error-bound estimation. Fourth, we reveal how noise augmentation training can provide high robustness to the method. Experiments show that our approach improves speed estimation accuracy over classical baselines while providing informative confidence estimates that indicate the reliability of individual predictions, even under adverse signal conditions.
items.title_ko: 재구성 기반 표현 학습을 통한 도플러 스펙트럼의 신뢰도 인식 지면 속도 추정
items.summary_ko: 이 연구는 지면을 향하는 도플러 스펙트럼을 사용하여 모바일 플랫폼(예: 철도 시스템)의 신뢰할 수 있는 지면 속도(speed-over-ground) 추정을 목표로 합니다. 기존 신호 처리 방식은 어려운 조건에서 성능이 저하될 수 있어, 재구성 기반 표현 학습을 통해 철도 도메인 데이터로 훈련된 신뢰도 인식 지면 속도 추정 모델을 제안합니다. 이 모델은 속도와 프레임 수준의 신뢰도를 동시에 추정합니다.
items.why_ko: 자율주행 및 모바일 시스템에서 환경 변화에 강인한 속도 추정 기술을 개발하여 안전성과 신뢰성을 높이는 데 기여합니다.

items.title: dbreunig/nesformer
items.body:
dbreunig/nesformer

Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen!

In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system:

Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed.

Followed by:

I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM.

Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow.

Via Hacker News

Tags: games, ai, generative-ai, llms, drew-breunig, qwen, conformance-suites
items.body_ko: dbreunig/nesformerDivyansh Agrawal의 qwenputer에서 영감을 받아, Drew Breunig는 Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU의 작동 에뮬레이터를 Qwen3.5-4B의 가중치에 심었습니다. 이제 Qwen 내에서 Super Mario Bros와 같은 NES ROM을 (매우 느리게) 실행하여 플레이할 수 있습니다!Hacker News의 댓글에서 Drew는 이 시스템을 구축하는 데 사용한 Opus 5.5 프롬프트를 공개했습니다.이 기사와 관련 소스 코드를 읽어보세요: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. 그런 다음 이 기술을 사용하여 Nintendo Entertainment System의 칩과 RAM을 에뮬레이션할 수 있는지 탐색해 보세요(오늘날 MISTR에서 FPGA로 하는 것처럼). 만약 가능하다면, 어떤 크기의 모델을 구축해야 하며, 더 작고 빠른 모델을 사용할 수 있다면 표준 클럭 속도로 실행할 수 있을까요?이어서 다음과 같은 내용이 있습니다.재미로라도 우리가 이걸 만들어야 한다고 생각합니다! 빠르지 않아도 괜찮습니다. 우리는 가중치와 ROM을 가리킬 수 있는 CLI를 원합니다.Opus는 Christopher Pow가 15년 전 공개한 NES CPU용 적합성 테스트 모음을 찾아 사용한 것으로 보입니다.Hacker News를 통해태그: games, ai, generative-ai, llms, drew-breunig, qwen, conformance-suites

items.summary_ko: Divyansh Agrawal의 'qwenputer'에 영감을 받아, Drew Breunig은 Qwen3.5-4B 모델 가중치 안에 Nintendo Entertainment System (NES)의 6502 CPU 에뮬레이터를 구현했습니다. 이제 Qwen 내부에서 '슈퍼 마리오 브라더스'와 같은 NES 롬을 플레이할 수 있으며, Drew는 Hacker News 댓글에서 이 시스템을 구축하는 데 사용된 Opus 5.5 프롬프트를 공개했습니다.

items.title: Was I wrong about open models & cyber risks?
items.body:
Last week coined the term “Black October“ after an onslaught of critical vulnerability disclosures, including PHP2Shell and GitLab, signified the moment when the cyber risks of AI models started to materialize. It seemed like the news cycle had stabilized a bit when I started writing this, but then there was news about another major crypto security incident at Binance. The crypto industry has a very long history of hacks, so it’s not the best industry to indicate vulnerabilities translating into new societal harm. Still, we are very much still living through the implications of this.
The best guess for what is happening in the cybersecurity space is that the behind the scenes work has only accelerated, bringing more people and resources in to try and patch the internet — the Wall Street Journal reported that cyber first responders are strained, which seems like the system working. We’re living through this plot of an exponential rise in vulnerabilities, which will take a long time to level off at the top of the sigmoid.

A few weeks ago, before the rapid acceleration in vulnerability disclosures and the uptick in reported hacks, I wrote the following take. It’s been getting a pretty consistent barrage of feedback, some hopeless dunk attempts and some reasonable discussion, so I wanted to unpack where I stand.
Share
Open-weight Mythos in April would’ve been fine?
When Claude Mythos was announced, it was previewed as if it was a new class of cyber weapon, where if it ended up in the wrong hands it would’ve caused mass societal destabilization.
It seems like this was wrong.
By all measures, GLM-5.3 is the model that crosses that threshold of capability, and there’s little public evidence that much has changed, and we’re over a month out of the model weight release.
In fact, I would go further. If Claude Mythos was accidentally released as open-weight, it seems like the world would have been more or less fine. Yes, there would be a clear increase in cybersecurity incidents and it would be bad for society if the model leaked, but it would be a scenario that looks more like an acceleration than a step change in risk.
The leading proponents of this new wave of open-weight fear mongering have effectively been making a falsifiable prediction — that the current open-weight models are going to cause substantial, not seen before AI harms by crippling our cyber infrastructure.
Based on all the evidence I have, which I’ve unpacked above, they’re set up to be wrong. At least now, after so many years of debating open weight risks, we will start to get some real answers.

To start the reflection, I wanted to do more due diligence and track down some receipts on the claim that the AI safety community was reacting as if open-weight Mythos would be an actual disaster, and not just a painful headache. This was distinctly my impression having lived through the online discourse. I’ve gotten criticism that the frontier AI community never said it would be a “true disaster,” but regardless of exactly what they said, it is always about how people hear and internalize your information.
Here are some examples of the sort of language that I felt was too exaggerated and from prominent people, which spilled into the public and more importantly federal government perspective that this was a cyber weapon include:
Rob Wiblin, host of the 80,000 hours podcast, on his own podcast (April 10, 2026): “If it fell into the hands of criminals or hostile state cyber actors, it would be an actual disaster.”

Anthropic, in the Project Glasswing announcement blog (April 7, 2026): “Given the rate of AI progress, it will not be long before such capabilities proliferate, potentially beyond actors who are committed to deploying them safely. The fallout—for economies, public safety, and national security—could be severe.”

For one that is actually more reasonable, to illustrate the fine lines between correct and exaggerated, from Zvi Mowshowitz (who I don’t agree with a ton of things on) on April 9, 2026: “Claude Mythos would give attackers a cornucopia of zero-day exploits for essentially all the software on Earth … It would be chaos.” To date, this chaos has been confined to those running large-scale digital products, which is good, but could change.
I largely still stand by my above writing a few weeks ago, but I’m nervous about it. I’m not a cyber expert, I’m working hard to make the most educated predictions I can. It’s a fine line between “all of our tech companies need to work extra hard to keep us secure” and “public infrastructure is actually going down.” It is very clear as of writing this that there are way more critical vulnerabilities which are being found in popular tools and fixes are being built.
For example, Epoch AI recently published a nice post on their internal work using GLM-5.3 to try and find vulnerabilities and chain them into what could be an attack. The actual exploit they found in Firefox is a good example of why cyber risks need multiple things to align for harm to be done:
We used GLM 5.3 to create a website that, simply when visited by a Firefox user and without further interaction, gave the attacker the ability to exfiltrate files from the user’s computer.

Here, the exploit is in Firefox, and a would-be hacker needs to plant a website that is looking for this exploit. This is doable, and could have serious consequences, but just finding the exploit is only one step in a multi-stage process.
In the previous post, I should’ve been more specific on what “fine” is for a future of cybersecurity, and in this case it means giving more credit to some of the AI safety community that discussed this reasonably as a new era in cyber instability. Reflecting on it, I’m not sure fine is the right word to describe what is inevitably coming – a forced industry update to a new way of working with software, which will clearly be expensive and accompanied by some hard work. If you’re already somber about the challenges coming from AI, I think fine is actually very suitable. If you didn’t price in a period of turbulence, fine undersells. I’ve written many times that I am in the former, difficulty will come, group — but I think humans are good at muddling through problems and patching immediate concerns.
What my view was closer to is that open models are providing balance in the offense-defense equation, and that Mythos coming sooner wouldn’t have massively upended this. I suspect most of these companies would be faster to adopt open-weight models than attackers, as most attackers are lower resourced than these companies. A key needle we’re watching the balance on is how willing attackers are to cause physical harm within the U.S. its allies. For now, while our adversaries have likely used these models and exploits to extract information en-masse in a clandestine way, it is not clear if there is a party who will cause mass harm by pushing the full force of these models at public institutions.
I thought this Tweet was a funny way to summarize some of the personnel / motive gaps in hacking:
Life is a lot easier once you stop seeing threat actors as hackers who want to break into systems by any means possible, and start seeing them as businesses with well defined business processes.

A bakery isn’t going to start making dog food because there’s a dog food shortage. ClickFix and Phishing actors aren’t going to drop everything to vibecode exploits just because a critical CVE came out.

The fact that the only actors exploiting this are the actors whose MO is exploiting things... isn’t a coincidence. It’s entirely predictable if you understand threat actor behavior.

items.title: [AINews] Building AIE CODE: The top Coding Agent Conference
items.body:
It’s a quiet day, so as we have done once per conference, we’ll do a behind the scenes look at AI Engineer, now serving 6M views a month for 1.8M monthly unique viewers.

CODE is the last flagship AIE of the year (there are also 2 partner conferences coming up - AIEi Shanghai takes place next week, and AIEi Sydney is a side event of NeurIPS in December). As a Summit it is meant to be more intimate: single track, invite-only for the top 1000 agentic engineers in the world (over 100k tuned into our Software Factories track at WF26).

My goal in curating AIE CODE is to try to recap the top themes of 2026 in code and gather the leaders of the industry to preview what’s next in 2027. Last year we had some absolute bangers building Skills and Software Factories, predicting the death of the IDE and of course the launch of Antigravity and Nano Banana Pro.

We have three themes this year:

Scaling without Slop: Last year’s call for No More Slop has resulted in lots of discussions about managing it this year, including the rise and fall of Tokenmaxxing. Our Scaling without Slop approach has mostly worked; we need more.

System One models: We believe S1 “smart software” is the largest change to AI Engineering that refreshingly explores the opposite direction to ever larger and more expensive and questionably productive swarms of coding agent FactoryFactoryFactories. While Diogo took pains to explain the difference between Decision Models and System One models on our podcast and his WF26 talk, it has largely been lost to the broader audience. Diogo and team TypeSafe are back for a mini “Jev Day” to show how System One models are truly being used by their top users.

Increasing Ambition: This year we also saw increasingly ambitious rewrites of some of the hardest categories of software, from browsers to Adobe PhotoShop Suite to mid-tier B2B SaaS. We’re excited to feature Jarred Sumner who will start from the rewrite of Bun in Rust and preview Bun AOT, new compiler features never before previously attempted particularly with this small of a team.

View post on X ↗

Of course, there’s way more to discuss this year from Cursor’s next phase as Grok Bot, to internal agents like Ramp Inspect, to the failure of Gas Town, and way way more we can’t fit in here.

Just trust me when I say I am extremely serious about doing justice to 2026, and that it has NOT been easy (for example we haven’t managed to secure a Muse Code speaker yet).

View post on X ↗

In any case, yes, we have a couple hundred seats left to fill and I’m making this plug to put you on notice to before we sell out (usually ~1-7 days before the event because that’s how people work in SF). If you are reading this far down in AINews, you’ve passed my test. Bypass the app for being a LS subscriber and join us!

$400 code for LS paid subscribers:

Use LS30 at checkout for 30% off :)

AI News for 10/28/2026-10/29/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!

AI Twitter Recap

Mistral Large 4 ("Le Chonk") Ships as Open Weights

Release: Mistral published updated open weights for its flagship model, aimed at agentic coding and cybersecurity, with customization through Mistral Forge (announcement, weights/blog).
Specs: 1.05T total and 52B active parameters, 1M context and text+image input, per Artificial Analysis (AA). Vals adds a 256K maximum output (Vals).

Pricing and license: $0.70/$2.10 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.07 cached), about 50% below the Preview. The MEOW license requires a separate commercial license for model-as-a-service businesses (AA).

Vendor claims: Mistral says it ranks #1 among open models on Cognition's FrontierCode, with cyber-defense testing by CrowdStrike, Cloudflare, Zscaler and others. A Mistral researcher reports a 64% human-preference win rate against GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 (@b_roziere, follow-up).

Independent evals: AA scores it 26 on Intelligence Index v5, narrowly the top open model developed outside China, 1 point above Muse Spark Open. It still trails DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM-5.3 by 6 points (AA).
Coding and agents: It scores 15% on FrontierCode 2.0, versus 29% for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and 22% for GLM-5.3. It reaches 25% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, versus 8% for Muse Spark Open. On the Coding Agent Index it scores 48 using 8.5M tokens per task, against 49 and 15.9M tokens for GLM-5.3.

Efficiency: It uses 82K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, 39% fewer than the Preview, which places it on the open-weights Pareto frontier. Cost is $2.06 per task.

Hallucination: The AA-Omniscience hallucination rate fell from 41% to 28%, but accuracy remains low at 26%.

Vals Index: #5 among open-weight models and #17 overall, with gains on app-building and legal research (Vals).

Architecture: According to a community analysis, the model uses full sparse attention in the style of DeepSeek V3.2 and GLM 5. It shares the KV cache across NoPE layers after layer 35 and shares indexers on RoPE layers from layer 17. It adds SSMax per-head logit scaling and LeRoPE (YaRN plus a learned per-frequency term), with no KV compression (@eliebakouch).

Day-0 ecosystem:
Serving: vLLM supports the FP8 and NVFP4 checkpoints with a built-in DSpark drafter, giving 1.92–2.23x output throughput (vLLM).

Local quants: Unsloth's 1-bit GGUF is 223GB, versus 1.1TB in FP8, retains 91% top-1 accuracy and runs on a Mac Studio (@UnslothAI).

Fine-tuning: TRL supports single-node LoRA SFT on 8×B300 at 142 GiB per GPU, processing 32.7K tokens per step in about 8 seconds (@_lewtun).

RL: SkyRL with vLLM ran LoRA RL on the NVFP4 checkpoint across 8 GB200 nodes. AIME 2024 rose from about 64% to about 75% in 75 steps (vLLM).

Cyber claims (unverified): One security researcher claims to have found four zero-days in a messaging app during two hours of testing. No details are public (@log4j).

Frontier Monitoring, Agent Safety and Offensive Cyber

OpenAI monitoring system: OpenAI now monitors all frontier RL runs, evaluations and internal Codex use. The system layers activation probes, reviewer models over reasoning and tool use, and investigator agents (OpenAI).
Hugging Face incident replay: Replaying that incident with the new monitors produced an alert about 30 minutes after the sandbox escape, more than 30 hours before the original breach.

September escape attempt: A model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Monitors flagged it within 15 minutes, and a human responder began reviewing three minutes later.

Paging: Frontier RL runs page humans 24/7 for urgent security alerts (@Eric_Wallace_).

Anthropic self-assessment: Since June, Claude has produced a preliminary misuse assessment immediately after each response. Anthropic says this has surfaced misuse that its classifiers were not designed to catch, and that it improves as the underlying model improves (Anthropic).

Open model exploits the patch gap: Epoch found that GLM 5.3 autonomously built Firefox exploits for six recent versions by reverse-engineering published but not-yet-shipped fixes (Epoch).
Cost and speed: Each compromised version cost about $1,000. The fastest attempt took 12 hours of a 48-hour budget.

New vulnerability: The model also found a previously unpublished bug, which Mozilla patched in Firefox 159.0.

Scope: Chrome attacks did not reproduce, but Epoch says that is not strong evidence of safety (details).

Supply-chain compromise: The official Claude Code VS Code extension was reportedly compromised. Pulling it during a brief window would have installed an SSH backdoor (@mattjay).

Agent tooling and detection:
safeagents: Hugging Face's open proxy blocks out-of-scope tool calls before execution, including metadata-endpoint requests, credential exfiltration and reward-file or verifier tampering (@yb2698).

WM-Basin: Meta FAIR's method uses API access
